Subject: TTFT & streaming SLOs — discovery recap and next steps

Hi Amit / Sarah,

Thanks again for the call today — good discussion. Quick recap of the performance requirements you shared and proposed next steps so we can scope a short pilot:

Summary of requirements (as we understood them)
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) target: <= 120ms p50, <= 250ms p95 for short responses (<= 60 tokens).
- Streaming: client-side UI expects streaming chunks; preferred transport is SSE but WebSocket is acceptable.
- Chunk cadence: ideally <= 250ms between chunks for conversational effect; maximum acceptable is 500ms.
- Concurrency/throughput: typical active concurrent users ~200, with 1.5x burst (300) at peak. Avg response size ~60 tokens; peak token throughput ~12k tokens/sec.
- SLO measurement: you care about 99th percentile TTFT under realistic concurrency and with cache misses.

Open clarifying items we need from you
1) Confirm whether SSE is a hard requirement or if WebSocket is acceptable.
2) Do you have client-side timeouts we should know about (e.g., 2s overall, 800ms TTFT)?
3) Can you share an expected concurrency distribution (e.g., % short vs long responses, session length)?

Next steps
- Rishi/Vivek to propose a quick test plan (baseline tests + pilot config).
- I will share a short spreadsheet to capture exact TTFT targets and cadence preferences.
- Schedule a 30–45m technical pilot kickoff next week to validate TTFT at scale.

Attaching a template spreadsheet for targets (will send in follow-up).

Best,

Thanks Marissa — this looks right. A couple quick clarifications from our side:

- SSE vs WebSocket: SSE is preferred because our web client integrates easily, but we can do WebSocket if it helps reduce overhead. Either works for us as long as chunk cadence is consistent.
- Client timeouts: our front-end will abort requests after 1.8s if no token arrives; so TTFT is critical.
- Accuracy vs latency: we prioritize perceived latency for chat UX. If there is a tradeoff between generating the first token fast and a small accuracy drop, we would accept that for short chat turns.

We can export a simple concurrency histogram from our analytics — will attach by EOD. Also, would like to see any recommendations for chunk sizes (bytes/tokens) vs cadence.

Hi Amit / Sarah — thanks for the clarifications, and good to know about the 1.8s client abort window. A few technical notes on how we approach TTFT + streaming:

1) Transport: SSE is simple (server->client) and works well with existing infra. WebSocket gives more flexibility (bi-directional) but TTFT is primarily influenced by model compute and request routing, not the socket.

2) Chunk cadence vs chunk size: smaller chunks (e.g., 1–8 tokens per chunk) with cadence <=250ms gives a smooth UX but increases per-chunk header overhead. For your case (short responses ~60 tokens) we typically stream every ~4–8 tokens or ~150–250ms to balance overhead vs interactivity.

3) TTFT drivers: cold model load, KV/prefix cache misses, placement jitter, and batching. To measure p95/p99 TTFT we recommend baseline runs with realistic concurrency (50, 200, 300) and a mix of cached vs uncached prefix workloads.

4) Measurement approach: we can run a short pilot hitting a dedicated test pool from our Hosted environment (or your Dedicated pool if you prefer). Deliverables: raw latency traces (TTFT per request), token cadence logs, and resource utilization. We'll surface p50/p95/p99 TTFT and chunk cadence distributions.

5) Quick resource estimate (rough): to meet <=120ms p50 and <=250ms p95 at 200 concurrent users for avg 60-token responses, expect to need 4–6 aggregate GPU slots depending on model size/quantization; we'll calibrate during pilot.

Action items for pilot prep
- Lumina: share concurrency histogram and any sample payloads (we need prompt length distribution).
- Redwood: we'll provide a test plan and prepare a short script that simulates SSE clients at different concurrencies.

I'll attach our internal TTFT playbook and a measurement checklist to the Drive link Marissa shared.

— Rishi
